rv.q: The ‘war’ section that takes up most of the play is, at its most intense, astonishing, a roiling living Guernica of nocturnal horror and nightmarish imagery.
This show remains a stunning piece of theatre: an immensely moving response to the futility of war.
He remains a masterpiece of creativity and connection.
This wondrous creature becomes the emblem of innocent suffering in the face of indescribable horror.
War Horse continues to be a stunning, invincibly spellbinding spectacle.
Even if you've seen it, this revival is still unmissable.
Does War Horse also still feature some of the most startlingly good stagecraft you will ever see?
Yes, it’s sentimental but this puppet-horsepowered tale of a stallion and his boy seeking each other through the carnage of the Somme, based on Michael Morpurgo’s book, remains tremendously moving.

This adaptation by Nick Stafford in association with Handspring Puppet Company is – on so many levels – a tour de force, heightened by the performances of actors who hold their own against the stunning visuals.
It earns its tears honestly, which is rarer than it sounds; grown adults leave looking like they’ve taken a part-time job chopping onions.
Through unrivalled stagecraft that pours care into every tiny detail, it tells the irresistibly moving story of a boy and his horse.
This is theatre and theatrical invention at its finest.
The show stands as a rip-roaring and astounding achievement in theatre and (bizarrely) looks fresher and more vibrant than it did nearly 20 years ago.
The production remains as powerful and impactful as ever.
War Horse remains relevant because big men still go to war, and a lot of people suffer for it. But as the remarkable and rather moving conclusion brings two old friends back together, hope remains.
Huge on spectacle but thin on drama, the revival of War Horse at the Olivier feels more like the launch of another tour than a seminal work that has returned with new resonance.
War Horse really is a beast of a show, and one that deserves its place in history.
So all the equine and puppetry magic is there, undimmed in two decades: a national treasure and global theatrical pride.
War Horse is just as magical and inspiring as it ever was.
Joey is magnificent, a puppet that doesn't attempt to hide the three humans controlling him yet utterly convinces you that he is indeed a horse.

All-in-all, these gripes with the script and acting choices don't take away from the overall power of the production, thanks to the sheer strength of the other elements, notably the puppetry, set design and score.
The production blends everything together, creating a tear-jerking story of the bond between human and animal.
This is a beautifully written, magnificently staged piece of theatre that has thoroughly deserved every success it has enjoyed.
Never for one moment did I think a production based on puppet characters could engage me emotionally but I was blown away from the very first moment of watching the foal onstage.

cn.t: Critics hail War Horse's homecoming as a triumphant return, with the groundbreaking puppetry remaining as magical and emotionally powerful as ever nearly 20 years later, proving this theatrical masterpiece has lost none of its impact.

ru.inst: Released Fridays at 1 PM via the National Theatre website (random queue). Until 30 July 2026.
